$doc: UI_SPEC §4, machine-readable. This file is the ONLY place a balance number lives.
Durations are written the way §4 writes them ('5m', '1d 12h') so this file can be
diffed against the spec tables by eye; sim/duration.ts parses them to ms.
Costs are maps so a level can charge two resources, which §4.2 does at Nv8.
A '$decision' field marks a number §4 did not give, and says why it is here.
Every '$'-prefixed key is documentation; sim/balance.ts reads none of them.
Changing a number here is a balance change: run `npm test` — the §4.2 storage
invariant is a build-failing check and it walks this file.
maxBuildingLevel is the Clash rule 'no building outranks the Town Hall'. It is what
keeps the storage invariant (§4.2) satisfiable: without it a level-1 island can reach
an upgrade whose cost is ten times any storage it can build.
baseStorage is the hall's OWN strongroom, and OPENING.md is why it exists: a day-one
island is the Ayuntamiento and nothing else, and `storeCap` sums store BUILDINGS — so
without this the first island can hold zero of everything and every payout, chest and
daily lands as nothing. Flat rather than a ladder: past the first Almacén (2 000) it is
noise, and its only job is to make the opening possible. Oro and madera only — ron and
metal still have to earn their store, which is the whole point of a store.

levels.$decision: Level 1 is only free for the copy the tutorial hands you (UI_SPEC 4.2 'free (tutorial)' / '(free)'). Applying it to every copy made placement a non-decision: extra producers and stores cost nothing and took no builder time, so a player could stamp the maximum allowed count instantly and the builder — the scarce resource the whole loop hangs on — was never spent. Additional copies cost resources and builder time; the granted one is seeded already built.

destileria.label: Destilería
destileria.$decision: count ladder — §4.2 gives the Destilería no allowed-count row

fundicion.label: Fundición
fundicion.$decision: count ladder — §4.2 gives the Fundición no allowed-count row
fundicion.$modelNote: Not bldg_foundry, and re-tested rather than taken on trust. The foundry now normalizes correctly in the model scene — SkeletonUtils rebinding fixed that — but ONLY under its 'action' clip. The island instantiates every building with clip 'idle', and the foundry's idle clip drives the very node carrying its 23x normalizing scale, so the fit is cancelled and it draws at 116 units across a 5-cell footprint. Verified from a [place] log, not inferred. A smithy reads as a metal producer, so the asset stays swapped.

almacen.label: Almacén
almacen.$decision: count ladder, and levels 7–8 — §4.2's store table stops at 6, which walls the player at Ayto 7 (see the invariant test)

Applying it to every copy made placement a non-decision: extra producers and stores cost nothing and took no builder time, so a player could stamp the maximum allowed count instantly and the builder — the scarce resource the whole loop hangs on — was never spent. Additional copies cost resources and builder time; the granted one is seeded already built.

banco.$decision: count ladder, and levels 7–8 — same reason as the Almacén

Applying it to every copy made placement a non-decision: extra producers and stores cost nothing and took no builder time, so a player could stamp the maximum allowed count instantly and the builder — the scarce resource the whole loop hangs on — was never spent. Additional copies cost resources and builder time; the granted one is seeded already built.

bodega.label: Bodega
bodega.$decision: §4.2 gives the Bodega capacities but no costs or times — these mirror the Almacén ladder shifted one rung cheaper

deposito.label: Depósito
deposito.$decision: §4.2 gives the Depósito capacities but no costs or times

muelle.label: Muelle
muelle.$doc: waterfront: the Muelle belongs ON the shoreline, so it is exempt from the buildable-plateau check the other buildings get.
$decision: cost and time — §4.10 fixes the 1m timer at beat 1:15, the cost is ours.
`ship: skiff` — round 12, and it is THE change that unwalls the game. Round 11's
playtest walked the whole cold path and never sailed: the starter hull hung off the
Astillero's first level, which sits behind hall 2, hall 3 and 5 000 madera — days of
idle check-ins before the half of the game RETENTION.md's loop closes through. The
design call: THE STARTER SKIFF SAILS FREE. The skiff is the Muelle's — build a dock
for 300 madera at hall 1 and there is a boat tied to it, in the first session, which
is the whole first-mate promise of OPENING.md. Everything that reads ship ownership
(sailLocked in ui/present.ts, hasShip in sim/tutorial.ts, sim/shipyard.ts) reads it
off level rows, so this one field is the entire mechanism. The Astillero now gates
BETTER HULLS, not sailing at all.

astillero.label: Astillero
$decision: the ladder — PLAN Fase 4's deep classes, Sloop → Galleon → Frigate → Marauder.
Level 1 is THE YARD ITSELF and carries no ship: the skiff is the Muelle's (see its
row — round 12's unwalling of the first sail), so the Astillero gates better hulls
rather than sailing. From level 2 up, each level IS the purchase of its `ship`
(sim/shipyard.ts reads ownership straight off level rows, so there is no second
ledger to drift), the costs are the long-arc gold sink RETENTION.md's days/weeks
clock asks for — 20k → 90k → 220k → 450k oro, each rung at least double the last —
and ron and metal ride along so both late resources keep a reason to exist. The
invariant test walks these against reachable storage at the hall level that opens
each rung. Level 1's 5 000 madera is a hall-3 project, not a wall: the sea has been
open since the 300-madera Muelle.

builders.$doc: §4.3 / §9: the game starts with TWO. One idle carpenter is the whole reason the free-builder nag exists.

$doc: §4.4. The golden rule wins over the table's first row: the last 5 minutes of ANY timer cost 1 gem, always, everywhere.

§4.4's three formulas are discontinuous at their own boundaries (1h reads 22 then 20; 1d reads 158 then 150), which would price a LONGER wait cheaper. sim/build.ts clamps each tier to the value the previous tier reaches at its ceiling, so the ladder only ever goes up. The published anchors 22/86/318 are unchanged.

chests.$doc: §4.5 — four slots from the start, only ONE unlocks at a time. That restriction is the pressure.

freeChest.$doc: The Cofre Libre is the MUELLE's, and only pays while the dock stands. It never mattered while every island began with one; OPENING.md's opening is the Ayuntamiento and nothing else, so it does now.

$doc: §4.6 — seven days, chained, day 7 visible from day 1.
§9: the streak PAUSES on a missed day, it does not reset.

quests.$doc: §4.7 — 3 active dailies, refresh at 04:00 LOCAL (§9: not midnight; midnight punishes the 23:55 player).

$doc: §4.7 and OPENING.md part 3, which is the one everybody forgets and is load-bearing:
without obstacles a day-one island is a vast void with a single building in the middle.
They cost 0 to clear, occupy one builder for a short timer, and pay a little madera —
so a brand-new player has something to do in their first thirty seconds that costs
nothing and teaches the builder-and-timer loop before any building is affordable.
The payout is sized off the opening it has to buy: a fresh island holds 250 madera and
an Aserradero Nv1 costs 300, so ONE cleared palm always tips the player over it. That is
the tutorial's first instruction — clear that tree, then put your Aserradero on the
ground it freed — and it has to be true rather than nearly true.
There is no respawn. Clash regrows them; we do not, because a field that grows back
into ground the player deliberately cleared is a system fighting the layout they made.
The field is the wilderness they tame once.

small.$doc: Palms and loose rock. Thirty seconds is a real timer and no wait at all, which is exactly what a first tap should be. The FLOOR of 50 is load-bearing: a fresh island holds 250 madera against a 300-madera Aserradero, so the very worst roll on the very first palm still buys it, exactly.

large.$doc: Wrecks and boulders. Fifteen minutes and a real payout — the first thing on the island worth planning around.

ranks.$doc: §4.7 — 3 divisions each, every division is +2% permanent offline production (+42% at cap).

xp.$doc: §4.7 — sqrt(build_seconds) per completed build, +10 per obstacle. Unlocks nothing on purpose.

$doc: §4.7 — the limit is the producer's own cap, never an artificial rule.
§3.22C — ≥72h away opens 'La Isla Resistió' instead of the normal HUD.

invariant.$doc: §4.2 STORE INVARIANT — build-failing test. Reachable capacity must clear the worst cost at that Ayuntamiento level by this margin.

placement.$doc: §3.15 build mode. `footprint` is how wide the MODEL is fitted, which is deliberately larger than the plot it stands on — the reference islands have roofs and jetties overhanging their neighbours. `plotFactor` is the fraction of that footprint two buildings may not share. 0.6 is the tightest value the shipped layouts already satisfy (the Fundición/Muelle pair sits at 0.667), so it rejects genuine overlaps without invalidating an island the renderer was tuned against. `clearance` is reference/SPACING.md's measurement made enforceable: on the shipped starter island no two structures touch and the gap between neighbours is on the order of a building's own width, because empty ground is what makes built ground legible. Two cells on top of the plots' own half-widths puts a full building-width of sand between two footprint-5 neighbours (centres 5 cells apart, plots 3 wide) while still letting the catalogue fit the 44 grid twice over.

$doc: PLAN.md Fase 2, measurable. Every number the open sea runs on lives here and
nowhere else, for the same reason the island's do: a balance you cannot diff is a
balance nobody can argue with. sim/sea.ts reads this file and invents nothing.
These numbers were MEASURED, not chosen. `node tools/voyages.mjs` plays hundreds of
seeded voyages with two models of player — a beginner who points the thumb and holds
it, and someone who has understood the ship — and prints survival, time to sink,
cargo landed and hull on arrival. Change anything below and re-run it; the headline
numbers are also asserted in tools/tests/sea.test.ts, so `npm test` fails if the sea
stops being playable.
What the table said before this pass, and why the pass happened: a beginner's FIRST
voyage — ring 1, the tutorial water — got home 68% of the time. Ring 2 was 30%, ring
3 was 5%, ring 4 was zero. Thirty seconds of open throttle sank three ships in four.
A third of all damage taken came from bumping into scenery. That is not a difficulty
curve, it is a drowning.
$harbour: How close to home, in cells, banks the hold — and how far out counts as having left.
`harbour` was 0.3 of a cell: sixteen units, smaller than the skiff's own turning
circle, so a player carrying a full hold had to thread a needle to bank it.
`departed` is the latch that stops a voyage reporting an arrival from the spawn,
which IS home water. It was 0.9 of a cell — but a seeded sea puts lootable islands
as close as twenty-two units from the harbour, so a player who left, took the first
thing they saw and came back had never armed it: no arrival, no way to bank the
hold, no way out of the voyage. One first voyage in eight, measured. sim/sea.ts now
also arms the latch on having taken anything, because carrying loot is proof you
went somewhere.
And that proof needed a floor under it, which cost another five voyages in four
hundred. Loot armed the latch WHEREVER THE SHIP WAS, and the nearest island in a
seeded sea is about forty-four units out with a loot reach of twenty-odd — so a
ship taking it from the near side arms the latch while still inside `harbour`, and
the next step reads a departed ship in ring 0 and ends the run two seconds after
¡Zarpar!. Both proofs now also require being outside the harbour, which is what
'somewhere else' has to mean. The test is 'taking the first island you see does not
end the voyage'.
`harbour` is also the number the HUD's compass switches to EN CASA on. It used to
keep its own 0.5 and was therefore announcing an arrival two and a half units of
sea before the hold would actually bank — believed, and wrong.

$doc: WHAT ACTUALLY REACHES THE STORES, AND WHERE THE VOYAGE ENDED.
Round 13's playtest, verbatim: 'The sea has no stakes and no decisions. Volver
banks the entire hold instantly from any distance and any hull state — I tapped
it at 200m out with the hull at 19% and kept everything, twice.' With no cost to
leaving and no cost to sinking, the whole risk/reward curve measured above never
reaches the player: every ring pays more and nothing charges for the trip back.
One rule answers it, and it is the oldest rule in seafaring: THE SEA CHARGES BY
DISTANCE. What the harbour takes off a voyage is the hold times `keep[ring]`,
read at the spot the voyage ended — so the ONLY way to bank a full hold is to
sail it into home water, which is the arrival sim/sea.ts already models with its
departure latch and its 'home' event. Inside `harbour` the share is 1: the last
twenty-five units of water are worth the whole tithe, and Volver at the dock is
free, which is what makes it a decision rather than a punishment.
`keep` is indexed by the HUD's own zone chip, so the number the player is
charged is the number they have been reading all voyage. The last entry repeats
outward forever, like `rings.bands`. 0.9/0.8/0.7/0.6/0.5 makes a ring-4 quit
cost 40% of the hold — measured against `loot`, about 120 units of a full skiff
— while a ring-1 turnaround, which is what a first voyage is, costs almost
nothing. Nobody is taught the game by being fined.
PLAN.md's line still binds: being sunk costs LOOT, never progress. Sinking
keeps half the hold rounded in the player's favour exactly as before, and the
share then applies to the half the crew are swimming with — so going down four
zones out keeps 30% where going down at the harbour mouth keeps 50%. Sinking is
therefore always exactly half of quitting in the same water, and quitting is
never the worse answer; a player can never be better off drowning.
`careen` is PLAN.md Fase 3's cheap-but-real repair, charged where the game can
actually charge it: a hull that goes down away from home is refloated and
patched, and the yard is paid out of what the crew saved. `rate` is a fraction
of the hull it is repairing — a skiff pays 60 units of a 150 hull, a marauder
224 — taken in `order` so it lands on materials before it touches the gold, and
stopping when the hold is dry. Never a debt, never a building, never progress.
It is zero inside the harbour for the same reason the share is 1 there: there
is nothing to refloat her from.
THE ISLAND HALF IS NOT BUILT AND IS NOT PRETENDED: a repair that persists
between voyages needs a field on GameState and a row on the Muelle sheet, which
are types.ts and ui/panels — not this round's files. What is here is the whole
cost the sea itself can charge, and it is charged every time.
'Distance is difficulty' is the whole risk/reward curve, and it was calibrated in
CELLS while it is experienced in SECONDS. At 17 units a second a cell goes by in
3.2 seconds, so a player holding the throttle for half a minute crossed NINE rings
and arrived in water designed to kill them, having made no decision at all.
`bands` is how many cell-shells each ring is thick, so the ring index — the number
the HUD's zone chip shows and the number every spawn and payout is drawn from —
advances at a pace a person can feel. The last entry repeats outward forever.
2,2,3,4,5 puts ring 1 at 4 seconds out, ring 2 at 11, ring 3 at 17, ring 4 at 27
and ring 5 at 40 — so the thirty-second run that used to end in ring 9 now ends
at the edge of ring 4, which is dangerous water a player chose to be in.
rings.$occupancy: Chance a cell holds anything at all. Rises with the ring: the sea gets busier as it gets worse, but never solid — an empty cell is what makes a full one feel like a find.

$doc: `damage`/`reload` are a BROADSIDE, one side at a time, and they were the reason
every fight was a losing trade. At 11 damage on a 2.1s reload a skiff needed 8.4
seconds to kill a kelpling and took 40 hull doing it; a hammerdead cost 12.6
seconds and more hull than the ship had. A fight nobody can win is not a fight.
`repair` is the one genuinely new rule, and it is what turns sinking into a
decision. With no way back from a bad fight, a hull is a countdown that started
the moment the player left, and every voyage ends the same way. After `calm`
seconds with nothing touching the ship the crew patches her at `repair` hull a
second — so breaking off, running for quieter water and coming back out is a real
play, and drowning means the player chose to stay.
$ladder: PLAN.md Fase 4's five classes. The skiff is the Muelle's — it comes with the
300-madera dock, day one, because the sea is the game's second half and a first
session that never sails never meets the game (round 12). The deeper four are
priced by the Astillero's level rows (the purchase is the upgrade;
sim/shipyard.ts reads ownership off level rows wherever they hang). The
shape of the ladder is one trade repeated: every rung buys HULL, GUNS and HOLD
and pays for them in HANDLING — turn, accel and turnDrag all get worse, so a
marauder is a fortress that answers the helm like a loaded barge. Top speed
creeps up (nothing in the sea makes more than 14, so escape stays a straight
line for every hull), but the dodge — the squid's strike window, a reef seen
late — keeps getting harder to make. The suite asserts the monotonics.
The balance fleets (tools/voyages.mjs) sail the SKIFF, so the asserted survival
table is the day-one experience and does not move with this ladder; the deeper
hulls are measured by tools/tests/shipyard.test.ts against the mob table: a
frigate two-shots the hammerdead a skiff needs four broadsides for, and it is
the first hull whose guns pay the squid's 340 in under ten volleys.
$rated: The deepest ring each hull is a MATCH for — one ring further out, the water
outranks the ship and sim/sea.ts raises its once-per-crossing 'zone-warning'
event, which the sea HUD turns into the line round 11's playtest asked for:
twin ring-3 hammerdeads took a skiff from 86% to 6% with no warning that
zones outrank the starter hull. Read against the measured fleet table
(node tools/voyages.mjs): a skiff comes home from rings 1-2 at 100% with the
hull barely marked, and ring 3 is where a fifth of the hull routinely stays
behind — so the skiff is rated 2 and the first warning is the 2→3 crossing,
exactly where the playtest got hurt. Each hull up the ladder is rated one
ring deeper; the rings tile outward forever, so even a marauder finds water
that outranks it. A warning, not a wall: the sim only speaks, the player
still chooses, and that choice is the whole risk curve.

$doc: Reefs were 28–42% of ALL damage taken, which is a game where a third of the
punishment comes from scenery. Two things were wrong. Damage was drawn from raw
speed, so a glancing scrape along a rock cost the same as ramming it head-on; and
there was no grace, so a ship held against a reef took a fresh hit every quarter
second — about 20 damage a second for as long as the thumb stayed down.
Now only the speed going INTO the rock counts, anything under `safeSpeed` of top
is free, and a contact cannot hurt again for `grace` seconds. Ramming a reef flat
out still costs a seventh of a skiff, which is what it should cost.
`deflect` is the other half, and it was the worse bug: a site was a wall that ATE
momentum, so a bow against a rock lost its way, and a ship with no way has no
rudder, so it stayed there. Measured: ninety seconds of open throttle in a
straight line covered 299 units of a sea where the ship does 17 a second — the
voyage was spent pinned to scenery. Now a rock turns the bow along its own face at
`deflect` radians a second and takes only the speed that was aimed at it, so
touching an island is a slide down its shore. Grazing a shoreline is a thing
players do on purpose; being welded to one is not a game.
`hp` is written against the skiff's 17-damage broadside so a kill is a countable
number of hits a player can feel: a blowfish is two, a kelpling three, a
hammerdead four. `damage`/`cadence` is what it costs to stand there and trade.
The squid is a lair guardian and is deliberately still out of a skiff's reach —
PRODUCTION.md §3 has the boss fight itself as unbuilt work. Its numbers are here
so that fight has something to be built against, not because a starting ship
should win it.

blowfish.$doc: Slow, harmless alone, always in a group — the ring-1 tutorial in monster form.

kelpling.$doc: Bites hard up close, so it punishes stopping.

hammerdead.$doc: Fast enough that turning away is a commitment, slow enough that a ship holding a straight line can break off — 14 against a skiff's 17, and a skiff at full helm only makes 12.

squid.$doc: The first boss. Guards a lair and does not leave it. Its bite row feeds the generic mob machinery nothing any more — the whole fight runs on `sea.boss` below — but speed/turn/sight/radius/hp are still read from here like any creature's.

$doc: The Giant Squid's fight — ROADMAP round 10's 'no phases, no tell, no reward
moment', answered with numbers a test can hold. The design is a rhythm with
three beats, each of them dodgeable ON THE STICK:
TELL. The squid never bites on contact. It casts: tentacles rise over a circle
of water (`strikeRadius`) marked `tell` seconds before they fall, and only a
ship still inside the circle when they land takes `strikeDamage`. The window is
sized against the hulls: a skiff under way crosses 19 units in 1.15s and walks
out of a 6.5 circle easily; a ship DEAD IN THE WATER accelerates through about
6 — just short. Sitting still is what gets you hit, which is the lesson.
PHASES. Under `frenzyAt` of its health the pattern changes: `volley` circles in
a line along your own course (`volleyLead` seconds of lead apiece), cast faster
(`tellFrenzy`) and more often (`cadenceFrenzy`). Holding your line now lands you
in the second or third circle — phase two is dodged by TURNING, which the big
hulls do worst, so the fight scales with the ladder instead of dying under it.
DIVE. A boss with a 30-unit strike against 54-unit guns is shelled from a deck
chair, so standing off is answered: beyond `strikeRange` it submerges — shots
pass over it — and closes at `diveSpeed` times its swim, surfacing `surfacePause`
before it can cast. Running leaves it behind (every hull outruns 14.7); parking
at gun range does not.
REWARD. The first squid killed on a voyage that is still owed one yields the
Cofre de las Profundidades, guaranteed, through the same stow() every site and
bounty pays, scaled by the lair's ring at `deepChestPerRing`. Once per season:
the claim is remembered outside the sim and handed back in as a flag on
startVoyage, because the sim keeps no calendar.
What patrols a cell, by ring. `[min, max]` enemies and the pool they are drawn
from; the last entry of each list repeats outward forever.
Ring 1 is tutorial water and reads like it: at most one blowfish in a cell, and
half the cells empty. Ring 2 introduces the kelpling, ring 3 the hammerdead, and
from ring 4 out the blowfish is gone entirely — the water stops being kind.
`tether` is how far past its site a guard chases before returning to its post. It
is what puts the danger ON the reward instead of scattered through the water
between: nothing in the sea is faster than a skiff at full way, so a threat you
can drive past is not a threat, and a threat standing on the thing you came for
is the decision the whole risk curve is made of.
It also has to be SHORTER than the ship's gun range, and that is not a detail. At
45 a guard would come out to 51-58 units against a skiff that shoots to 54, so
there was no distance from which a player could fight on their own terms: every
defended site had to be charged, and a pilot that stood off and cleared the guards
first measured WORSE than one that barrelled in. Positioning is the skill PLAN.md
Fase 2 asks for, and a leash longer than the guns is what makes it impossible.
$post: How far off its site's shore a guard stands. It has to be INSIDE the water the
player must enter to take the site (`loot.reach` plus the two radii, about twelve
units off the shore) or the whole arrangement is decorative: guards posted at 7 to
22 units could be looted around at full way, and measured across a fleet a ring-5
voyage taking five defended sites lost sixteen hull in total. Guards hugging the
shore of the thing they are guarding cannot be skirted, only fought or run past.
patrols.$roam: How far from its own patch an open-water patrol follows before turning back. Long enough to be a chase, short enough that leaving its water ends it.
patrols.$openChance: Chance a cell with nothing worth guarding carries a lone patrol anyway. Danger belongs ON the reward — but open water with nothing at all in it is a corridor, not a sea.

$doc: What a sunk creature leaves floating, straight into the hold.
There was nothing here at all, and that was a hole underneath the entire combat
system. The cannons fire themselves — PLAN.md Fase 2 asks the player to play
positioning rather than a fire button — so the ONLY reason to turn a beam onto
anything was to stop it biting, and running was always cheaper than that.
Measured over a fleet, a pilot that fought whatever came at it came home with
LESS cargo than one that drove straight past, at every ring. The central verb of
the game was a net loss.
Sized against a site: three hammerdeads pay about a third of what the island they
are guarding does, so clearing a defended site is worth doing and is never worth
more than the site itself. The squid is a boss and pays like one.
ROADMAP round 10: 'a site is taken by sailing over it, which is the placeholder,
not the design.' Wrecks are now a BEAT: come inside loot reach and a boarding
party rows over — `seconds` of it — and the cargo comes back as a burst only if
the ship is still on station when they return. Drift more than `slack` units
past the loot reach and the party rows back empty; returning starts the clock
from zero, so boarding is a commitment rather than a drive-by.
The tension knob is what the sim already does: mobs keep closing the whole
time, the guns keep firing on their own, and nothing stops the hull taking
bites — so boarding under fire is a choice with a price on it. Wrecks only:
an islet or a grove is picked clean from the deck, but a wreck has an inside.
4.5 seconds is ~2.6 bites from a kelpling standing on the site, against wreck
loot that is the gold-richest in the sea — checked by the fleet table, which
held its survival curve with this on.
What a site pays, before the ring multiplier `1 + ring * perRing`. A ring-1 site
is worth about 120 units of cargo and a ring-4 site about 300, against a hold of
900 — so a first voyage comes home with something, and a deep one comes home with
a hold full or does not come home at all.
$reach: How close to a site's shore the ship has to come to take it, on top of the two
radii. It used to be 3, which is less than the ship is long — so taking anything
meant RAMMING it, and the reward mechanic was also the biggest source of damage in
the game. Measured: a beginner lost six times more hull to scenery than to
monsters at every ring. At 10 a ship that sails up to an island collects it, which
is what sailing up to an island should do.

$doc: OPENING.md: the map is LARGE AND FIXED from day one, Clash-style — it never grows under
a player's feet, so there is no save migration and no plateau that moves.
reference/SPACING.md measured the size: the eleven buildings need 283 cells for their
footprints alone, a 26 grid offers 255, and a 44 grid offers ~911 — 31% coverage, which
is where the shipped game sits.
obstacleRadius is a MEASURED number, not a taste. src/sim/ owns no terrain (render/
island.ts generates it, and the sim may not import three.js), so the obstacle field is
seeded inside the largest superellipse that is buildable for EVERY seed. 0.49 is that
radius, measured over twenty seeds at grid 44 and re-checked by
tools/tests/obstacles.test.ts against the real generator. A scene that knows its own
terrain can widen the field with `reseedObstaclesInPlace`.
